land.cliopatria: Sovereign Principality of the United Netherlands
land.text: the northern Netherlands of the Sovereign Principality (Cliopatria 1814 shape, 35,750 km2)

predecessors.note: The Sovereign Principality page: 'the reunification was finalised on 16 March 1815' when William Frederick 'was proclaimed King William I of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands in Brussels'. The southern Netherlands came to William as Governor-General from 1 August 1814 and are not in Cliopatria's 1814 shape.

capitals.name: Amsterdam
capitals.note: Infobox: Amsterdam 'Capital and largest city', The Hague 'Government seat'; the article calls Amsterdam the 'nominal capital' and says The Hague holds the States General, cabinet and Supreme Court (The Hague: 4.3007 E, 52.0705 N). The UK of the Netherlands page does not mention alternating capitals.

minus.text: the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg as it stood before 1839: today's Luxembourg and the Belgian province of Luxembourg

correction.text: the United Kingdom of the Netherlands without the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg; the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg was a German Confederation member in personal union with the Dutch king, so it is taken out of the Dutch outline and drawn in the lighter tint by the vassal_start/vassal_end events

keyframe_review.note: 71,126 km2 against the infobox 68,095 km2 for the United Kingdom of the Netherlands (ratio 1.04, fine). The shape holds the northern Netherlands, the former Austrian Netherlands and Liege, and the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg; the Grand Duchy was 'placed in personal union with the Netherlands, though it remained part of the German Confederation', so the correction takes it out and the ledger draws it as a tint (1815-1890).

minus.text: the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg as it stood before 1839: today's Luxembourg and the Belgian province of Luxembourg

correction.text: the United Kingdom of the Netherlands without the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg; the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg was a German Confederation member in personal union with the Dutch king, so it is taken out of the Dutch outline and drawn in the lighter tint by the vassal_start/vassal_end events

keyframe_review.note: 71,104 km2, identical in extent to 1815-1819 (3 extra cells at most). Same correction: the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg is a personal-union partner and German Confederation member.

minus.text: the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg as it stood before 1839: today's Luxembourg and the Belgian province of Luxembourg

correction.text: the Netherlands of 1830-1833 without the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, whose western part Belgium claimed and held until the 1839 treaty

keyframe_review.note: 45,829 km2: the northern Netherlands plus the whole Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, i.e. the Dutch king's claim, with Belgium gone. The Belgian Revolution page: 'Belgium was declared an independent state' (4 October 1830) while 'the Dutch army ... held onto Maastricht' and kept the Antwerp citadel to 23 December 1832; Belgium 'claimed the entire Grand-Duchy of Luxembourg' (Grand Duchy page), so the western part is contested to 1839 and the whole Grand Duchy is taken out of the direct outline.

correction.text: the Netherlands of 1834-1839 with Maastricht, which the Dutch army held through the revolt, and Venlo; the rest of Limburg was Belgian-held until 1839

keyframe_review.note: 37,108 km2: the shape drops Luxembourg and about 5 cells of Dutch Limburg around Maastricht (southernmost latitude 51.18 N, while Maastricht lies near 50.85 N). The Belgian Revolution page: 'The Dutch army, however, held onto Maastricht, and as a result, the Netherlands kept the eastern half of Limburg'; the Duchy of Limburg page says the duchy of 1839 was Limburg 'minus Maastricht and Venlo', which stayed with the Netherlands, so those two fortress towns are added back.

correction.text: the Netherlands (with the Duchy of Limburg) without the Luxembourg rump, which is a personal-union partner

keyframe_review.note: 40,699 km2 (1840-1865): modern Netherlands (incl. all of Dutch Limburg after the 1839 partition) plus the rump Grand Duchy of Luxembourg. The Treaty of London page: 'the Province of Limburg was split into Belgian and Dutch parts' and the Grand Duchy 'lost' a large part to Belgium; the rump stayed in personal union with the Dutch king and joined the Zollverein in 1842. The Duchy of Limburg (1839-1867) was a German Confederation state under the Dutch king; it is drawn as Dutch land here. The Luxembourg rump is drawn as a tint by the ledger.

correction.text: the Netherlands without Luxembourg, which remained in personal union until 1890

keyframe_review.note: 40,721 km2. 1866-1870: the German Confederation collapsed in 1866 ('led to the collapse of the German Confederation', Duchy of Limburg page) and the Second Treaty of London (11 May 1867) affirmed Limburg 'an integral part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands' and Luxembourg's independence and neutrality (Grand Duchy page). Luxembourg stays a personal-union partner until 1890.

40,723 km2 for 1871-1916, but the Grand Duchy's personal union ended in 1890 ('the Dutch monarchy ceased to hold the title Grand-Duke of Luxembourg'), after which Luxembourg is a state of its own (Cliopatria 'Luxembourg' row from 1890). The Netherlands row keeps Luxembourg's cells to 1916, which is wrong from 1890; Cliopatria drops them in 1917. Correction: remove Luxembourg for the whole span (1871-1889 it is the tinted partner, 1890 onward foreign).

38,405 km2 (lowest latitude 50.71 N): the modern Netherlands without Luxembourg, which agrees with the Luxembourg row. The infobox total of 41,865 km2 (incl. 18.41 percent water) is 9 percent above Cliopatria's land-based figures (ratio 0.92 for 38,295), fine. Unverified for 1917-1939: page budget; the page says nothing of boundary changes.
38,318 km2: a 0.2 percent change from 1917-1921 that no page opened explains (the land reclamation of the Zuiderzee is a candidate but is not on the pages opened). Unverified: page budget.
38,449 km2, within 0.4 percent of 1922; no page opened explains the change. Unverified: page budget.
38,382 km2, southern edge 50.78 N: a rounding-level change; no page opened explains it. Unverified: page budget.
37,537 km2, 2.2 percent below 1930-1935; no page opened explains the drop. The shape is the territory that the German invasion of 10 May 1940 found. Unverified: page budget.

correction.text: the Netherlands of 1939, occupied by Germany from 10 May 1940 and run as a Reichskommissariat, not annexed

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for 1940-1944, which Cliopatria lacks for the Netherlands: its 'Nazi Germany' shapes of 1940-1944 contain 155 of the Netherlands' 157 cells as German land. The occupation page says Germany invaded on 10 May 1940, the Dutch forces surrendered on 15 May, and Seyss-Inquart took power as Reichskommissar on 29 May 1940; the page 'does not say the territory was annexed' (incorporation into a Greater Germanic Reich was a 'long-term aim'). So the land stays the Netherlands' under occupation (hatched, rule 4); the government and Queen Wilhelmina went to London (13 May).

38,382 km2: the Netherlands after the liberation (first Dutch city, Maastricht, liberated 13-14 September 1944; the German surrender at Wageningen on 5 May 1945). Cliopatria starts the row again in 1945; the 1944 liberation of the south is not drawn.

38,295 km2 for 1950-2023. The Netherlands annexed 69 km2 of German border land on 23 April 1949 (Elten, Selfkant, Suderwick) and returned it on 1 August 1963 except the Duivelsberg (about 3 km2); at under one 250 km2 cell this does not show in Cliopatria's grid, so the shape stands.
38,295 km2, same as 1950-2023; infobox total 41,865 km2 (land 33,500 km2) so Cliopatria's figure sits between land and total (ratio 0.91 of the total); fine.

region.text: the northern Netherlands of the Sovereign Principality, from 1813

ledger.note: 1815: William Frederick is proclaimed King William I of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands in Brussels. 'the reunification was finalised on 16 March 1815 when William Frederick was proclaimed King William I'; the Netherlands page infobox dates the United Kingdom of the Netherlands 16 March 1815.

region.text: the former Austrian Netherlands and the Prince-Bishopric of Liege, without the western Grand Duchy of Luxembourg (today's Belgian province of Luxembourg), which was the personal-union Grand Duchy's (ledger 2)

ledger.note: 1815: the southern Netherlands are joined to the kingdom. 'William Frederick was awarded with the former Austrian Netherlands' by the Eight Articles of London (21 June 1814) and 'became Governor-General of Belgium on 1 August' 1814; the union of north and south was finalised 16 March 1815. The page does not name a previous state (Cliopatria has none for 1814), so 'nobody'. The UKN page adds Liege as part of the fusion. [Reviewer eu-20-k, 2026-10-31: region now excludes the Belgian province of Luxembourg, as keyframes 0-2 and the vassal_start of May 1815 do; it had been both direct and personal-union land.]

region.text: the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg as it stood before 1839: today's Luxembourg and the Belgian province of Luxembourg

ledger.note: 1815: William I gains the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg in personal union. 'William agreed to cede the Principality of Orange-Nassau and parts of the Liege to Prussia on 31 May 1815', and in exchange 'gained the Duchy of Luxembourg', 'placed in personal union with the Netherlands, though it remained part of the German Confederation'. A personal union, not a vassalage in law; drawn as the lighter tint.

region.text: the citadel of Antwerp

ledger.note: 1830: Dutch troops keep the Antwerp citadel inside the new Belgium. The page gives the citadel (kept after the revolution; the Dutch bombarded the town from it) but no day for the start.

region.text: the francophone western part of the Grand Duchy, later the Belgian province of Luxembourg

ledger.note: 1830: Belgium claims the whole Grand Duchy of Luxembourg. 'it claimed the entire Grand-Duchy of Luxembourg as part of Belgium'; 'The Dutch king and Prussia rejected this claim because they wanted to keep the fortress.' The page does not say who held the countryside; the zone is the western part that the 1839 treaty gave to Belgium.

region.text: Limburg, of which only Maastricht (and Venlo) stayed Dutch until 1839

ledger.note: 1830: the Dutch army holds Maastricht and the rest of Limburg is disputed. 'The Dutch army, however, held onto Maastricht, and as a result, the Netherlands kept the eastern half of Limburg.' The page gives no date for the start of the dispute; the zone is Limburg east of the Meuse, which Belgium held in practice.

region.text: the Belgian provinces, without the western Luxembourg that is a separate dispute

ledger.note: 1830: Belgium secedes. 'The Belgian Revolution broke out on 25 August 1830' and 'The Provisional Government then issued a Declaration of Independence on 4 October 1830' (the page's lead gives 27 September). The Netherlands keep Maastricht and the Antwerp citadel for a time.

region.text: Belgium, invaded on 2 August 1831

ledger.note: 1831: the Dutch army invades Belgium (Ten Days' Campaign). 'On 2 August 1831 the Dutch army, headed by the Dutch princes, invaded Belgium.' The page does not list the ground taken.

region.text: Belgium after the Dutch withdrawal

ledger.note: 1831: the offensive fails after French intervention. 'Marshal Etienne Maurice Gerard crossed the border with 70,000 French troops under his command on 9 August'; the United Kingdom page says the offensive 'failed after French intervention'. The end day follows from the campaign's name ('Ten Days'), 2 to about 12 August.

region.text: the citadel of Antwerp

ledger.note: 1832: the Antwerp citadel falls. 'Gerard returned to Belgium in November 1832 with the Armee du Nord and besieged the citadel taking it on 23 December 1832.'

region.text: the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg as it stood before 1839: today's Luxembourg and the Belgian province of Luxembourg

ledger.note: 1839: the Grand Duchy is partitioned. 'The treaty partitioned the grand duchy'; it 'lost two-thirds of its territory to Belgium's new Province of Luxembourg' (the Grand Duchy page says 'more than half'); the rump stayed in personal union under William I. The old extent of the vassal tint ends here and the rump follows.

region.text: Belgium's new Province of Luxembourg, formerly the western Grand Duchy

ledger.note: 1839: the western Grand Duchy passes to Belgium. 'The treaty partitioned the grand duchy' and the francophone western part went to Belgium (Treaty of London, 19 April 1839). The land was the personal-union partner's, not direct Dutch land; recorded so that the Belgian dossier's gain has a pair.

region.text: the western Grand Duchy

ledger.note: 1839: the Treaty of London ends the Luxembourg dispute. 'The treaty ... was signed on 19 April 1839 between the major European powers'; 'The Dutch recognised Belgian independence, in exchange for territorial concessions.'

region.text: the Dutch part of the Province of Limburg

ledger.note: 1839: Limburg is split and the Dutch part confirmed. 'the Province of Limburg was split into Belgian and Dutch parts'; the Dutch part became the Duchy of Limburg inside the German Confederation under the Dutch king, 'minus Maastricht and Venlo' (Duchy of Limburg page). Cliopatria redraws the Dutch outline for 1840, a year after the treaty.

region.text: Limburg east of the Meuse

ledger.note: 1839: the Limburg dispute ends. The Netherlands keep Maastricht and the eastern half of Limburg; 'From 1839 onwards [Limburg is] divided into the Belgian province of Limburg and the Duchy of Limburg.'

region.text: the rump Grand Duchy of Luxembourg

ledger.note: 1839: the rump Grand Duchy remains in personal union with the Dutch king. 'the rump covering one-third [or, per the Grand Duchy page, less than half] of the original territory' stayed in personal union with the Netherlands under William I; it joined the Zollverein in 1842 and the Second Treaty of London (1867) affirmed its independence and neutrality.

region.text: Luxembourg, a separate state from 1890

ledger.note: 1890: the personal union with Luxembourg ends. 'A succession crisis ended the Dutch monarchy's claim to the title': 'the Dutch monarchy ceased to hold the title Grand-Duke of Luxembourg', and Adolph of Nassau-Weilburg founded the Grand Duchy's own monarchy. The page gives no day; Cliopatria's Luxembourg row starts in 1890.

region.text: the whole Netherlands

ledger.note: 1940: Germany invades and occupies the Netherlands. 'Nazi Germany invaded the Netherlands on 10 May 1940 as part of Fall Gelb'; the Dutch forces surrendered on 15 May, the government and royal family 'fled to London', and Seyss-Inquart took power on 29 May 1940 at the head of a Reichskommissariat. This state is the occupied party; the occupier is the counterpart.

region.text: the whole Netherlands

ledger.note: 1945: the Netherlands are freed. 'The Wehrmacht commander in the Netherlands, Blaskowitz, surrendered at Wageningen on 5 May' 1945, Liberation Day; the south had been freed from September 1944 (Maastricht 13-14 September). The page also gives 8 May for the final German capitulation and, in one section, 6 May for the signing.

union.text: Elten, a small town on the Rhine

region.text: Elten, Selfkant and Suderwick

ledger.note: 1949: the Netherlands annex German border land. At noon on 23 April 1949 Dutch troops moved to occupy 'an area of 69 km2': Elten (19.54 km2), Selfkant (41.34 km2) and Suderwick (0.64 km2). Germany was under Allied occupation, and the page names no German state; below the grid's cell size.

region.text: Elten, Selfkant and Suderwick, except the Duivelsberg

ledger.note: 1963: the annexed land is returned. 'On 1 August 1963 the territory was returned to West Germany, except the Duivelsberg/Wylerberg hill (about 3 km2), which remains Dutch', after the Treaty of The Hague of 8 April 1960 (280 million marks).

region.text: Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, the Caribbean Netherlands

ledger.note: 2010: the Caribbean Netherlands join the country proper. Infobox 'Caribbean reorganisation: 10 October 2010'; 'Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba were incorporated as special municipalities, collectively known as the Caribbean Netherlands'. Mirror of netherlands-antilles' loss of 10 October 2010. About 330 km2 overseas, outside Cliopatria's European outline. [Added by reviewer eu-20-k, 2026-10-31.]

wars.name: Belgian Revolution
wars.outcome: Belgium became independent (declared 4 October 1830) and the Treaty of London of 19 April 1839 recognised it; the Netherlands kept Maastricht and eastern Limburg and the Grand Duchy was partitioned.
wars.note: The Antwerp citadel was lost on 23 December 1832; the frontier was fixed in detail by the Treaty of Maastricht (1843) according to the United Kingdom page.

wars.name: Ten Days' Campaign
wars.outcome: The Dutch offensive failed after French intervention of 9 August 1831; the page names no ground kept.
wars.note: The page gives the invasion (2 August) and the French crossing (9 August) but not the Dutch withdrawal date.

wars.name: Battle of the Netherlands
wars.outcome: German victory; the Dutch forces surrendered on 15 May 1940 after the bombing of Rotterdam and the country was occupied until 1945.
wars.note: Invasion 10 May 1940 as part of Fall Gelb; the queen and government left for London (13 May).

wars.name: Liberation of the Netherlands
wars.outcome: Allied forces entered at Mesch on 12 September 1944, Maastricht was the first city liberated (13-14 September) and the German surrender at Wageningen on 5 May 1945 freed the whole country.
wars.note: Operation Market Garden began 17 September 1944; Hunger Winter 1944-45.

certainty.note: The Congress of Vienna and the 1815 constitution fix the kingdom; the Luxembourg frontier is a German Confederation border.

Belgian frontier de facto and disputed until the Treaty of London of 19 April 1839; the detailed line was fixed by the Treaty of Maastricht (1843), so 1839-1842 is a settled but not yet surveyed frontier.
Treaty frontiers with Belgium and Germany; the 1949-1963 German border annexation and the 1940-1945 occupation are the exceptions.

notes:
Page budget 9 used (UKN, Belgian Revolution, Treaty of London 1839, Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, Netherlands, Sovereign Principality, German occupation, Duchy of Limburg, Dutch annexation of German territory).
LUXEMBOURG. Cliopatria draws the Grand Duchy inside the Netherlands shape for 1815-1829 and 1840-1916 (11 cells; 29 before 1839 with the Belgian province of Luxembourg), and keeps those cells to 1916 although the personal union ended in 1890. This dossier removes it from the direct outline and draws it as a personal-union tint with counterpart 'luxembourg' (vassal_start 1815, vassal_end 1839 for the old extent, vassal_start 1839, vassal_end 1890). The 'luxembourg' dossier (Cliopatria row 1890-2024, eu-20) should start in 1815 or the Grand Duchy 1815-1890 needs its own dossier; duchy-of-luxembourg ends in 1443 and says it is a different state, so no merge exists.
NOT DRAWN. The Treaty of Maastricht (1843) fixed the Belgian frontier; the page gives no change. Zuiderzee and other reclamation (the small area changes in Cliopatria 1922-1936) are not on the pages opened. The rulers list was not collected (the pages give only 'William I 1815-1839' for the United Kingdom; William II and III are not on them), so identity.rulers is omitted. The Kingdom Charter of 15 December 1954 (Netherlands, Suriname, Antilles as countries of the Kingdom) is not a border event for the European Netherlands; the colonies have their own dossiers (dutch-east-indies, dutch-suriname).
1940-1944. Cliopatria's Nazi Germany shapes 1940-1944 contain the Netherlands (155 of 157 cells) as German territory; the occupation page says it was run as a Reichskommissariat, not annexed. The nazi-germany dossier (eu-21) should show the Netherlands as occupied, not owned. A new keyframe netherlands_1940 (1940-1944) is written here.
COUNTERPARTS. 'allied-occupied-germany' (1945-1949) has no dossier; the 1949 German land belonged to the Allied-occupied zones, and West Germany (federal-republic-of-germany, 1950) took it back in 1963. 'luxembourg' as above.
Gazetteer names the gazetteer lacks: Venlo, Elten, Selfkant, Suderwick.
Dates that differ between pages: the Belgian declaration of independence 4 October 1830 in the body, 27 September in the lead; German surrender 5 May (Wageningen) with 8 May for the final capitulation and 6 May in one section.
